screens.title: What is AWS Systems Manager?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Systems Manager is a grouped set of operational capabilities that let you automate routine tasks, maintain consistent configurations, and centralize investigation across EC2 and hybrid servers. At its core it provides remote command execution, state enforcement, patch automation, workflow automation, and aggregated operational insights. For a solutions architect this matters because it converts manual, error-prone processes into repeatable, testable actions. For example, rather than logging into servers individually to check disk usage or install a monitoring agent, you can run a single command that executes across a fleet and returns structured output. Systems Manager depends on an agent installed on managed instances; the agent communicates securely to the service and enables features like Run Command and State Manager. A common misconception is that SSM replaces monitoring or configuration management tools entirely — it complements them. SSM focuses on operational control and remediation, while monitoring tools surface metrics and alerts. The core takeaway is simple: SSM turns operational procedures into scalable, auditable automation. Think about your most repetitive operational task and ask whether it can be expressed as a command, an association, a patch baseline, or an automation document — that framing will guide how you adopt SSM.

screens.title: SSM Run Command
screens.narratorSegment: Run Command allows you to send commands or scripts to one or many managed instances without requiring SSH or RDP. It runs through the SSM Agent on each instance, securely executes the provided commands, and stores structured output you can view in the console or push to CloudWatch or S3. A typical use is ad-hoc diagnostics or fleet-wide changes during a migration: for example, run a shell script to collect disk and memory stats, or install a monitoring agent. Start by targeting a small set of non-production instances to validate the script and parameters. A common mistake is using destructive commands without testing; always include safety checks in scripts and use comments describing intent. Run Command also supports parameters and document names, such as the AWS-provided AWS-RunShellScript. When managing multiple accounts, cross-account role configuration allows Run Command to reach instances in other accounts. The core steps are: prepare the script, select targets, run with a document, collect outputs, and analyze results. Ask yourself what outputs you need before running a command so you collect the right logs and avoid re-running destructive operations.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › SSM Run Command
Run Command flow
1. Prepare script and parameters
Write the script with validation, avoid destructive operations, and include logging to stdout/stderr for collection.
2. Select targets
Choose instances by ID, tags, or resource groups. Test first on a small non-production set.
3. Execute and collect
Run the document and review outputs in the Command history. Optionally forward to CloudWatch or S3.
Common mistake
Running untested destructive commands across production fleets can cause widespread outages. Always test and use safeguards.
Key Takeaway

Run Command is your primary tool for safe, centralized ad-hoc execution. Plan outputs and test before wide deployment.

Concrete example
Collect disk and memory info on a set of web servers by sending a shell script that runs df and free, then examine the outputs in Command history or S3 for post-analysis.
Quick checklist
  • Test on non-production instances.
  • Log outputs to CloudWatch or S3 when needed.
  • Use parameterized documents to avoid hard-coded values.

screens.title: Run Command: Example and safety
screens.narratorSegment: Here we walk through a concrete Run Command example and discuss safe usage. The example invokes the AWS-provided document that runs a shell script on a managed instance and returns standard output. The script in this demonstration lists processes, disk usage, memory, and the hostname — useful diagnostic data during an incident. When you send the command, the SSM Agent executes it and the service records per-instance output accessible from the command history. Important safety practices: first, run on a staging target or a single instance; second, avoid commands that modify files or restart services unless you have a tested rollback; third, include logging and exits so you can detect failures automatically. A common misconception is that collecting diagnostics is risk-free — some diagnostic commands may still trigger high input and output or reveal sensitive data if outputs are shared widely. Use scoped permissions for S3 destination buckets and limit who can run commands. After viewing outputs, clean up any temporary resources such as S3 objects if they contain sensitive details. Run Command: Example and safety means always test run command scripts on non-production instances and restrict output destinations and permissions to avoid accidental data exposure.. In practical terms, a concrete command, outputs, and safety checklist. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Run Command Example
Example command
aws ssm send-command \ --instance-ids "i-0abcdef1234567890" \ --document-name "AWS-RunShellScript" \ --parameters 'commands=["ps aux", "df -h", "free -h", "hostname"]' \ --comment "Gather diagnostics"
Expected outputs
  • Process list for troubleshooting load.
  • Disk usage to check free space before deployments.
  • Memory usage metrics for sizing decisions.
Safety checklist
Test targets first
Run on a single staging instance to validate commands and outputs before fleet-wide execution.
Limit outputs
Choose CloudWatch or S3 destinations carefully and restrict access to sensitive outputs.
Rollbacks and logging
Include idempotent scripts and logging to detect and revert unintended changes.
Key Takeaway

Treat Run Command like any privileged operation: test, log, restrict outputs, and plan rollbacks.

screens.title: SSM State Manager
screens.narratorSegment: State Manager provides continuous enforcement of a desired configuration by associating documents with target instances. An association names the desired state, the document that applies it, the schedule or trigger, and the targets. This is ideal for preventing configuration drift in multi-tier applications: define one association for web servers to maintain a specific Apache configuration, another for application servers to ensure a specific Java runtime, and another for database servers to keep security agents installed. State Manager periodically checks and enforces the desired state, remediating drift automatically. A common misconception is that State Manager instantly solves all configuration problems; it enforces what you specify, so correct and minimal documents are required. If associations are too broad or apply heavy changes, you can inadvertently cause repeated disruptions. Best practices include scoping associations to resource tags, using test windows, and monitoring compliance reports. Think of State Manager as a guardrail: it maintains and enforces policies so that drift doesn't silently accumulate and escalate troubleshooting time after a migration or change window. SSM State Manager means use state manager to declare and enforce desired configurations across instance groups and prevent configuration drift.. In practical terms, define associations to maintain desired configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › SSM State Manager
How associations work
Association components
Document, targets (IDs or tags), schedule or trigger, and parameters that define the desired state.
Example scenario
Ensure all web servers have the approved Apache config file; State Manager checks and reapplies the correct file on schedule.
Misconception
State Manager enforces specified state; it will not guess desired values. Incorrect associations can cause repeated failures if not scoped or tested.
Practical tips
  • Scope associations by tags to avoid unintended targets.
  • Use testing windows and start with low-frequency checks.
  • Monitor compliance reports and refine documents gradually.
Key Takeaway

Define minimal, tested associations and enforce them to reduce drift. State Manager is best for continuous enforcement, not one-off fixes.

screens.title: When to use Run Command, State Manager, or Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between Run Command, State Manager, and Automation comes down to intent and frequency. Use Run Command when you need ad-hoc execution: troubleshooting, collecting diagnostics, or running one-off updates. An example is executing a diagnostic script during an incident across a small set of instances. Use State Manager when you need continuous enforcement of a desired configuration: it applies associations on a schedule and remediates drift automatically. For multi-tier apps that must always have a specific configuration, State Manager is the right tool. Use Automation when you need a repeatable workflow that chains multiple steps or AWS A P I calls — a runbook as code. Automation fits blue/green deployments, automated remediation that restarts services and then validates health, or creating AMIs and updating launch configurations. A misconception is thinking Automation replaces the other two: Automation often orchestrates Run Command and State Manager steps as part of a larger sequence. When designing solutions, ask whether the task is ad-hoc, continuous enforcement, or a multi-step workflow; that question will point you to Run Command, State Manager, or Automation respectively. In practical terms, choose the right ssm capability for the task. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Capability Comparison
Run Command — Ad-hoc
Best for diagnostic scripts, quick fixes, or one-time updates. Example: gather df and free outputs during an incident.
State Manager — Continuous
Declare desired state and enforce it periodically to prevent drift. Example: enforce correct Apache config across web tier.
Automation — Orchestration
Chain steps and API calls for multi-step workflows. Example: automated remediation that restarts an instance, validates health, and creates an OpsItem if failure persists.
Decision guide
  1. Is the task one-time or ad-hoc? Use Run Command.
  2. Is it continuous enforcement? Use State Manager.
  3. Is it a sequence of steps or requires branching? Use Automation.
Integration note
Automation documents can call Run Command and reference State Manager compliance as part of a broader runbook. They are complementary, not exclusive.

screens.title: SSM Patch Manager
screens.narratorSegment: Patch Manager automates the process of updating operating systems and approved applications across managed instances. It uses patch baselines to decide which patches are approved or rejected, and patch groups and maintenance windows to schedule when patches are applied. For architects this is important because automated patching reduces the window of exposure to known vulnerabilities and ensures consistent security posture across fleets. A typical pattern is to define baselines that match organizational policy, assign instances to patch groups that map to environment types, and schedule non-peak maintenance windows. Common pitfalls include setting windows too narrowly so patching fails repeatedly, or approving all patches without evaluating compatibility with applications. Patch testing and phased rollouts help avoid disruptions. Another misconception is believing Patch Manager eliminates the need for testing; automated patching should be combined with staging validation and monitoring. The practical workflow is: define baselines, group instances, schedule windows, run patching, and review compliance reports to track success and troubleshoot failures. SSM Patch Manager means use baselines, groups, and windows to keep instances patched while minimizing operational risk through testing and phased rollouts.. In practical terms, automate os and application patching with baselines and windows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › SSM Patch Manager
Patch Manager essentials
Patch baselines
Define which patches are approved for your environments and which should be rejected.
Patch groups and windows
Map instances to groups and schedule maintenance windows to control when patching runs.
Phased rollouts
Apply patches to a small group first, validate, then expand to reduce risk.
Operational checklist
  • Define baselines aligned to security policy.
  • Schedule windows in off-peak times and notify stakeholders.
  • Test patches in staging and roll out gradually.
Key Takeaway

Patch Manager enforces a consistent and auditable patch strategy, but must be paired with testing and phased deployments to avoid disruption.

screens.title: SSM Automation Documents
screens.narratorSegment: Automation documents are runbooks expressed as JSON or YAML that sequence SSM actions and AWS A P I calls. They let you codify routine maintenance, deployments, or automated remediation so that a multi-step process runs reliably and consistently. For example, a blue/green deployment runbook can create new instances, apply configuration with State Manager, use Run Command to install an application, switch traffic, validate health, and roll back if checks fail. Automation documents may be triggered manually, on a schedule, or in response to events like alarms. A misconception is to treat Automation as only for simple tasks; it is built for complexity and branching logic, including input parameters and error-handling steps. Best practices include parameterizing documents for reuse, adding validation steps, and attaching approvals for high-risk actions. Also, attach detailed logging and create OpsItems when an Automation step fails so responders have context. screens.title: Lab: Use Run Command to gather system information
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through using Run Command to gather system information from an EC2 instance. Begin by launching an instance with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore IAM profile attached so the SSM Agent can communicate with Systems Manager. Verify the agent is running on the instance; for Linux use the systemctl status command to confirm the agent process. Next, confirm the instance appears as a managed node in Fleet Manager; it may take a few minutes after launch. When the instance is visible, prepare a short diagnostic script that runs df -h, free -h, and hostname — these commands provide disk, memory, and identity details. In the console choose the AWS-RunShellScript document, paste the commands, and target the test instance. Keep CloudWatch or S3 output enabled if you want to collect results centrally, remembering to secure any S3 bucket you use. Run the command, then open the command history, select the command ID, and review instance-specific output. Finally, terminate the instance to avoid charges. A common mistake is not validating IAM permissions; ensure the instance profile includes the managed core policy. This exercise demonstrates how quickly diagnostics can be collected at scale without SSH.

screens.title: SSM Agent and hybrid management
screens.narratorSegment: The SSM Agent is the software running on EC2 instances and on-premises servers that enables Systems Manager features. Installing and verifying the agent is the first operational prerequisite. For Linux, check the agent service status and ensure the instance has an instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore so the agent can authenticate to Systems Manager. In hybrid environments, the agent enables on-premises servers to appear as managed nodes by registering them in Systems Manager with the appropriate activation and IAM permissions. A frequently overlooked point is permissions scope: the instance profile must allow the agent to call the required SSM APIs and to upload outputs to destinations like S3 if configured. A typical operational checklist is: install agent, attach the correct IAM role or activation, verify node appears in Fleet Manager, and test a simple Run Command to confirm end-to-end communication. Misconfigurations commonly surface as nodes not appearing in the console or commands timing out; these usually trace back to agent status, network reachability, or IAM permissions. The closing question to consider is: before automating at scale, how will you validate agent presence and permissions across your environment?

In this lesson we explore AWS Systems Manager as the centralized toolset for automating operational tasks across EC2 instances and on-premises servers. You will learn what each capability does, why it matters for reliability and security, and how these pieces fit into a professional architect’s operational playbook. We’ll cover remote command execution without SSH, continuous configuration enforcement, automated patching, runbooks as code for repeatable workflows, and the consoles that aggregate operational data and incidents. For example, instead of manually logging into dozens of servers after a migration to update a configuration file, you can use a single SSM Run Command to update the file across a fleet and collect outputs centrally. We’ll also emphasize safety: test commands on a non-production set, define patch baselines that match policy, and use Automation documents to codify complex procedures so they execute reliably. By the end of the lesson you’ll understand the core SSM capabilities and how they combine to reduce manual effort, minimize human error, and help maintain compliance across a distributed environment.

In the next minutes you will acquire concrete, verifiable skills with Systems Manager that map directly to operational needs. First, you will learn how to use Systems Manager to centralize operational control for EC2 and hybrid instances so that you can manage large fleets with fewer errors. You will practice Run Command for secure, cross-instance scripting without SSH, and you will learn how to test commands safely before broad rollout. Next, you will work with State Manager to define and enforce desired configuration states, preventing configuration drift for multi-tier applications. Finally, you will configure Patch Manager to automate security updates and align patch baselines to organizational policy. Each objective includes why the skill matters and a short mnemonic to help recall the intent. These competencies are designed as verified milestones: after completing the activities you will be able to demonstrate each capability in a staging environment and explain when to use it in a migration or operations plan.

This second objectives slide focuses on runbooks, insight tools, and safe operational practices. You will learn to author SSM Automation documents — runbooks as code — that chain SSM steps and A P I calls to automate remediation or deployments. You will also explore SSM Explorer and OpsCenter for aggregated operational visibility and central incident handling, so you can see patch compliance and OpsItems across accounts and regions. Additionally, you will verify SSM Agent installation and managed node status, a necessary operational check before relying on SSM capabilities. Finally, you will integrate automation into migration and incident plans, using Automation documents and OpsCenter runbooks to scale common operations. Each skill includes a short mnemonic or scenario to anchor the concept and a verified milestone so you can demonstrate the capability in a live or staging environment.

AWS Systems Manager is a grouped set of operational capabilities that let you automate routine tasks, maintain consistent configurations, and centralize investigation across EC2 and hybrid servers. At its core it provides remote command execution, state enforcement, patch automation, workflow automation, and aggregated operational insights. For a solutions architect this matters because it converts manual, error-prone processes into repeatable, testable actions. For example, rather than logging into servers individually to check disk usage or install a monitoring agent, you can run a single command that executes across a fleet and returns structured output. Systems Manager depends on an agent installed on managed instances; the agent communicates securely to the service and enables features like Run Command and State Manager. A common misconception is that SSM replaces monitoring or configuration management tools entirely — it complements them. SSM focuses on operational control and remediation, while monitoring tools surface metrics and alerts. The core takeaway is simple: SSM turns operational procedures into scalable, auditable automation. Think about your most repetitive operational task and ask whether it can be expressed as a command, an association, a patch baseline, or an automation document — that framing will guide how you adopt SSM.

Run Command allows you to send commands or scripts to one or many managed instances without requiring SSH or RDP. It runs through the SSM Agent on each instance, securely executes the provided commands, and stores structured output you can view in the console or push to CloudWatch or S3. A typical use is ad-hoc diagnostics or fleet-wide changes during a migration: for example, run a shell script to collect disk and memory stats, or install a monitoring agent. Start by targeting a small set of non-production instances to validate the script and parameters. A common mistake is using destructive commands without testing; always include safety checks in scripts and use comments describing intent. Run Command also supports parameters and document names, such as the AWS-provided AWS-RunShellScript. When managing multiple accounts, cross-account role configuration allows Run Command to reach instances in other accounts. The core steps are: prepare the script, select targets, run with a document, collect outputs, and analyze results. Ask yourself what outputs you need before running a command so you collect the right logs and avoid re-running destructive operations.

Here we walk through a concrete Run Command example and discuss safe usage. The example invokes the AWS-provided document that runs a shell script on a managed instance and returns standard output. The script in this demonstration lists processes, disk usage, memory, and the hostname — useful diagnostic data during an incident. When you send the command, the SSM Agent executes it and the service records per-instance output accessible from the command history. Important safety practices: first, run on a staging target or a single instance; second, avoid commands that modify files or restart services unless you have a tested rollback; third, include logging and exits so you can detect failures automatically. A common misconception is that collecting diagnostics is risk-free — some diagnostic commands may still trigger high input and output or reveal sensitive data if outputs are shared widely. Use scoped permissions for S3 destination buckets and limit who can run commands. After viewing outputs, clean up any temporary resources such as S3 objects if they contain sensitive details. State Manager provides continuous enforcement of a desired configuration by associating documents with target instances. An association names the desired state, the document that applies it, the schedule or trigger, and the targets. This is ideal for preventing configuration drift in multi-tier applications: define one association for web servers to maintain a specific Apache configuration, another for application servers to ensure a specific Java runtime, and another for database servers to keep security agents installed. State Manager periodically checks and enforces the desired state, remediating drift automatically. A common misconception is that State Manager instantly solves all configuration problems; it enforces what you specify, so correct and minimal documents are required.
